options.label: Culture, Society and Social Research
options.labelReason: Social theory, cultural history and material culture supply the substantive core. Qualitative and quantitative courses support empirical inquiry.
options.concept: Study how communities create meaning and organise social life. Combine social theory, cultural history and material culture with qualitative research and statistics.
progression: Introductory sociology precedes qualitative inquiry and modern social theory. Modern Sociology precedes advanced social theory. Research Methods & Statistics adds empirical design and quantitative analysis.

options.label: Migration, Identity and Inequality
options.labelReason: Social theory, histories of empire and gender, rights, media and collective action illuminate identity and inequality.
options.concept: Study how migration, empire and social institutions shape belonging. Use histories of race and gender, sociology, media and human rights to examine inequality and collective responses.
progression: Introductory sociology precedes qualitative inquiry and modern social theory. Modern Sociology precedes advanced social theory.
options.distinctness: This option gives greater weight to rights, migration, gender, representation and collective action, with dedicated historical and social-psychological perspectives.

options.label: Global Change, Communities and Sustainability
options.labelReason: Sustainability and environmental science support questions about how communities and institutions respond to global change.
options.concept: Study how communities and institutions respond to global change. Combine social research, governance and environmental science to examine sustainability debates, collective action and policy.
progression: Sustainability foundations precede the advanced environmental course. Introductory and modern sociology precede advanced social theory. Qualitative inquiry and applied communication add complementary ways to study and engage communities.
options.distinctness: This option adds sustainability, ecology, environmental processes and applied climate communication to the shared social-science core.

analysis: The culture option connects introductory and modern sociology, civil society and cultural interpretation to material culture, African heritage and historical inquiry. Qualitative Research Methodology covers interviews, ethnography, observation, thematic coding and reflexivity in a team project. Research Methods & Statistics now contributes study design, sampling, inference and regression. These are substantive overlaps, with no equivalent to Utrecht’s prolonged supervised ethnographic fieldwork. The migration option studies rights, colonialism, race, gender and inequality through legal frameworks, history, media and social psychology. Native American Histories supplies Indigenous and colonial perspectives, and Youth Resilience to Extremism supplies identity and belonging mechanisms in its specific context. The sustainability option joins social theory, environmental justice, climate communication and environmental science. Governance of Sustainability examines institutions, power, justice and participation. Persuasive Communication uses real sustainability projects and field reflection, complementing public engagement without claiming ethnographic training. Description-only Social Movements & Environmental Justice, the history research seminar, literary interpretation and climate communication provide supported disciplinary and methodological contributions. The three plans differ pairwise by six, eleven and ten courses in each direction. The sustainability science courses explain environmental processes and support the global change option without themselves teaching anthropology.

alignment.rationale: Both introduce comparative study of culture, society and social organisation.
Both develop theoretical analysis of social ordering and meaning.
UCR studies contemporary social theory, including civil society and social movements. Utrecht traces the history of anthropological theory as a discipline.
UCR uses historical evidence to study gender, sexuality and activism in North America. Utrecht studies gender and sexuality through comparative anthropology.
No UCR course in the selected union directly reproduces the anthropology of lived religion, media and popular culture.
The comparator's dedicated scientific-writing elective remains unmatched rather than being equated with a broader communication course.
UCR addresses race, inequality and representation across several courses. Utrecht offers a dedicated anthropology elective on national identity and racialisation.
Both examine transnational structures and global interdependence; the comparator grounds these in everyday sociocultural complexity.
Both examine violence, security and conflict; the comparator emphasises situated ethnographic perspectives.
Both introduce research design and statistics. UCR adds a team data project.
Both develop a research design and use qualitative evidence. Utrecht’s proposal prepares a dedicated ethnographic fieldwork sequence.
The comparator's applied mixed methods and statistics component remains unmatched.
The comparator's dedicated ethnographic field-methods course has no full UCR equivalent.
Utrecht requires supervised fieldwork, with each student collecting evidence for their own part of the project.
Utrecht assesses each student individually on a thesis written in pairs. UCR displays optional independent research alongside it.
This major elective extends ethnographic fieldwork and analysis in the same block as BAP 3.
Profiling choices remain open. At least 15 EC must be at intermediate level or above.
UCR examines sustainability systems and governance. Utrecht uses anthropology to analyse how people experience sustainability problems.
UCR studies ecological processes and environmental governance. Utrecht focuses on the relationships between humans, non-human life and political power.
